---
title: "Research"
---

I study how culture and institutions shape economic and political development, using large-scale historical data and field experiments.

## Publications

::: {.paper}
[How Cultural Diversity Drives Innovation: Surnames and Patents in U.S. History](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/739323){.paper-title}

::: {.paper-meta}
with [Jonathan Schulz](https://sites.google.com/site/jonathanfschulz/) and [Joseph Henrich](https://henrich.fas.harvard.edu) · [Journal of Political Economy]{.paper-venue}, 2026, 134(4): 1245–1305
:::

::: {.paper-summary}
Using a surname-based measure of cultural diversity in U.S. counties from 1850 to 1940, we show that rising diversity increased both the quantity and quality of innovation — by expanding the range of ideas available for recombination and fostering the social interactions that spread them.
:::

::: {.paper-links}
[PDF](files/Posch_Schulz_Henrich_Cultural_Diversity_Innovation.pdf) [Journal](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/739323) [Replication package](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/EXE7CK) [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/stuartanderson/2023/10/18/immigration-and-diverse-populace-made-america-an-innovation-superpower/)
:::
:::

::: {.paper}
[The Political Economy of Propaganda: Evidence from U.S. Newspapers](files/Ottinger_Posch_PoliticalEconomyOfPropaganda_December_2025.pdf){.paper-title}

::: {.paper-meta}
with [Sebastian Ottinger](https://sites.google.com/view/sebastian-ottinger/) · [Journal of the European Economic Association]{.paper-venue}, accepted
:::

::: {.paper-summary}
Can racial outrage in the media be manufactured by elites for political gain? Using high-frequency newspaper data from the late nineteenth-century U.S. South, we find evidence consistent with Democratic elites orchestrating a racist propaganda campaign through local newspapers — and benefiting from it at the polls.
:::

::: {.paper-links}
[PDF](files/Ottinger_Posch_PoliticalEconomyOfPropaganda_December_2025.pdf) [Replication package](https://zenodo.org/records/21452316) [Broadstreet](https://www.broadstreet.blog/p/bad-ngrams)
:::
:::

## Working papers

::: {.paper}
[On the Importance of African Traditional Religion for Economic Behavior](files/Butinda_Lameke_Nunn_Posch_SanchezDeLaSierra_African_Traditional_Religion.pdf){.paper-title}

::: {.paper-meta}
with Lewis D. Butinda, [Aimable A. Lameke](https://marakujakivuresearch.com/organization/), [Nathan Nunn](https://nathannunn.arts.ubc.ca), and [Raul Sanchez de la Sierra](https://raulsanchezdelasierra.com) · Reject & resubmit, [Econometrica]{.paper-venue}
:::

::: {.paper-summary}
Beer sellers in the eastern DRC overestimate the risk of theft and hold too little inventory as a result. Randomly-timed access to commonly-used protective rituals corrects these beliefs among sellers who believe in their efficacy — raising inventories, sales, and profits.
:::

::: {.paper-links}
[PDF](files/Butinda_Lameke_Nunn_Posch_SanchezDeLaSierra_African_Traditional_Religion.pdf) [BFI research summary](https://bfi.uchicago.edu/insight/research-summary/on-the-importance-of-african-traditional-religion-for-economic-behavior/)
:::
:::

::: {.paper}
[Doux Commerce: Markets, Culture, and Cooperation in 1850–1920 U.S.](files/Posch_Raz_Doux_Commerce.pdf){.paper-title}

::: {.paper-meta}
with [Itzchak Tzachi Raz](https://www.tzachiraz.com/)
:::

::: {.paper-summary}
As railroads integrated American markets between 1850 and 1920, counties gaining market access developed more universalist, tolerant, and trusting cultures — with more impersonal cooperation and less reliance on kin-based support.
:::

::: {.paper-links}
[PDF](files/Posch_Raz_Doux_Commerce.pdf) [Marginal Revolution](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2025/07/markets-culture-and-cooperation-in-1850-1920-u-s.html) [National Affairs](https://www.nationalaffairs.com/blog/detail/findings-a-daily-roundup/crossing-culture)
:::
:::

::: {.paper}
[Do Disasters Affect the Tightness of Social Norms?](files/Winkler_jmp.pdf){.paper-title}

::: {.paper-meta}
New draft coming soon
:::

::: {.paper-summary}
Combining data on conflicts, epidemics, and natural and economic disasters with global survey data, I show that disasters tighten social norms — an effect that can persist for decades and is transmitted to the next generation.
:::

::: {.paper-links}
[PDF](files/Winkler_jmp.pdf)
:::
:::
